title: Artemis - Ready For Flight
description: Select cuts from the short film "Artemis - Ready For Flight" which features NASA employees who were involved in the testing of the Orion Capsule at NASA Glenn's Armstrong Test Facility.
keywords: GRC-2022-CM-0104, Cale Yeager, Steve West, Erin Reed, Monica Hewitt, Nicole Smith, Artemis, Media Relations, Neil A. Armstrong Test Facility, Orion, Plum Brook Station, Spacecraft, Staff, Space Environments Complex, AVAIL, SEC, Videographer of the Year Entry
via: the NASA Image and Video Library

transcript.text: I think every person who comes to work for NASA dreams of being part of that spacecraft
development program that you get to see at launch, if you get to see it send humans to
the next step in the frontier of space, right?
And I think every one of us started with NASA with that dream.
Well, I've been out here 12 years.
I'm a research laboratory mechanic.
They hired me on actually general labor and said if I did really well, I had a chance to
get into the NASA apprentice program.
So I did really well and I got into the program.
They sent me to school and then on the job training hours to learn the skills that I needed
for here.
I'm Kayleigh Eager.
I'm part of the research laboratory mechanic apprenticeship program.
Okay, my name is Steve West.
I'm the test facility coordinator here at SEC.
I think I'm starting my 37th year.
If you want to do the math, I think it's pretty close to that.
My name is Erin Reed.
I'm a test engineer here at SEC.
I'm Nicole Smith.
I'm the project manager for Orion testing here at NASA's Plumbwork Station.
For the better part of the last 12 years, I've been working on some form of Orion.
It's always been very intrigued by space.
I incline mechanically and go with my hands.
I like buildings that stop troubleshooting.
So it kind of worked out that I got to partner my skills with my desires and what I enjoy.
I would say my main rollout here is an operator, especially during test time.
I run the compressors for the cryo-troud that changes the temperatures in the vacuum chamber.
I really like the people I work with, everybody I work with.
We're all working together towards a common goal.
So there are lots of disagreements that we have, technical disagreements.
We may see things with a different perspective, but we all know that it's because we're trying
to create the best solution.
Data is our product.
We don't make any widgets or anything, so that's our product.
So I believe the engineering and the techs here are outstanding.
I would put them up against anyone in the world.
When it's a flight vehicle, you're not just concerned about the data from the test, you're
actually concerned about the vehicle itself.
When you get in the test conditions and you've got the chamber pumped down and the crowd
shrouds of the temperature is supposed to be, to me it's exciting.
You're part of the crew, you're part of history really, so I think that's very neat.
I really feel it's a really awesome thing to be part of.
We are taking that next step.
We are doing that next great leap.
We face challenges almost daily, which is part of why I love this job.
I mean, we keep our crew working very effectively all the time, which is a challenge, and I get
excited about this.
The idea of the first woman stepping foot on the moon and me getting the opportunity to
work on this spacecraft here, it's huge, so I'm really excited for that.
